newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity rises with temps, higher cash.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity rises with temps, higher cash.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were trading higher Tuesday, taking strength from hot, humid weather, stronger physical power prices and rumors of outages at two western generation facilities, industry sources said.
"The dailies (spot prices) are going really high, it's the heat that's keeping daily prices strong," said one Western futures trader.
Sources also said rumors were circulating that two 700 megawatt (MW) generation units at the Colstrip coal-fired plant in Montana were out of service following a lightning strike.
Furthermore, rumors were also circulating regarding a possible outage at the Four Corners generation facility in New Mexico, although no further details were available.

As of 1235 EDT, September Palo Verde (PV) was trading up $1.86 at $32.90 per megawatt hour (MWh) after hitting a new contract high of $33.25 and a low of $32.50 per MWh. October was up 53 cents at the day's high of $23.70 following a low of $23.50 per MWh.

September California Oregon Border (COB) was trading up 65 cents at $25.00 following exchanges at $24.75-25.05 per MWh, while October was up $1.16 at a new contract high of $23.30 after reaching a low of $22.50 per MWh.
NYMEX said as of 1150 EDT an estimated total of 445 PV and 149 COB contracts had traded.

In cash business, next-day firm, peak prices at PV were said to have traded as high as $95.00 per MWh from early Tuesday talk at $55.00-65.00 per MWh, while those at COB jumped more than five dollars on the day to $29.75-30.75 per MWh.

Much of the western U.S. was predicted to feel sweltering heat through Thursday with the exception of Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico, which were expected to experience much cooler than normal conditions.
In the six to 10 day forecasts, temperatures in the Southwest would cool toward more seasonal levels, while those in the Northwest would stay near to slightly above normal.

Separately, the operating limit on the Pacific Intertie transmission system will be increased to 6,900 MW from the current interim rating of 6,300 MW from 2400 PDT Tuesday, Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) said.

The spokeswoman for the federal agency which operates the intertie said only 6,650 MW of energy could be scheduled on the system after the capacity increase. The difference between the operating and scheduling limits was said to be a step to help manage curtailments due to loop flow problems.
The 6,900 MW limit will continue until the next seasonal operating plan is put together and reviewed by the Western System Coordinating Council.
Also, electricity output from the 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 3 in Wintersburg, Ariz., held at 90 percent power early Tuesday for repairs to a condensate pump.
The unit was expected to return to full power within the next 48 hours, a spokesman for the plant said.
The adjacent 1,221 MW Palo Verde nuclear power unit 2 was operating at 91 percent of capacity as of early Tuesday as the unit coasts down to a scheduled refueling outage September 6.
Water flow into regional hydroelectric systems in the Northwest and Canada has been slowed in recent days to refill reservoirs for fish migration requirements.
PV open interest for August 4 rose 155 to 5,254 while COB open interest fell 20 to 5,166, NYMEX said.
